name: SSRF and Server-Side Request Risks
intent: When your server fetches a URL that a user supplied, the user is borrowing your server's network position. Restrict what it may reach, check the address it really connects to, and do not blindly follow redirects.
scenario: A photo app lets users import a picture by pasting a link, and lets customers register a webhook address that the server calls. Both features make the server send a request to an address chosen by someone else.
problem: A server usually sits inside a trusted network. It can reach things the internet cannot: internal admin tools, databases, other services and, on cloud platforms, a metadata endpoint that can hand out credentials to the machine. If the server fetches whatever URL it is given, a stranger can aim it at those places and read the answer or trigger an action. This is server-side request forgery (SSRF). The obvious checks, such as refusing the word localhost, are easy to walk around.

howItWorks.title: Why the inside is reachable
howItWorks.text: The request leaves from your server, so the network treats it as your server. Firewalls that block outsiders from internal addresses do not block it. Some internal services also trust any caller on the inside, so they never ask for a password. The attacker needs no access of their own, only a feature that makes your server fetch a URL.

howItWorks.title: A deny-list is a guess at what is bad
howItWorks.text: A deny-list refuses known bad targets such as localhost or the metadata address. The same address has many spellings (a whole number, shortened or alternative notations, IPv6 forms), a harmless-looking hostname can resolve to a private address, and a public page can answer with a redirect to one. Every spelling you forgot is a hole, so a list of bad things is always incomplete.

howItWorks.title: An allow-list names what is good
howItWorks.text: Only fetch hosts you have chosen: your image CDN, a partner's documented domain. Match the exact host after parsing the URL, not with a substring test, and only allow http and https. It is the strongest simple control, at the price of maintenance when a legitimate new host appears.

howItWorks.title: Check the address you connect to, and connect to that address
howItWorks.text: Resolve the name yourself, refuse private, loopback and link-local results, then connect to the address you checked. If you check one DNS answer and the HTTP client looks the name up again, a record with a very short lifetime can return a public answer to the check and a private one to the fetch. That trick is called DNS rebinding. Pinning the checked address closes the gap.

howItWorks.title: Handle redirects and limit the blast radius
howItWorks.text: A redirect can send the fetcher somewhere you never checked, including from an allowed host that has an open redirect. Either do not follow redirects, or run every hop through the same checks. Around the code, run the fetcher with the fewest network rights (egress rules that allow only what it needs), cap response size and time, do not return raw responses to the user, and require a token for the cloud metadata service where the platform offers one.

pros: An allow-list plus a checked, pinned address removes the whole class of attack, not individual payloads
Network egress rules protect even when the application code has a bug
Cloud metadata protections, such as session-token requirements, reduce the damage of any single miss
The same fetcher guard serves every feature that calls out: import, preview, webhooks, PDF rendering
cons: An allow-list needs upkeep, and every new legitimate source is a request to someone
Correct address checks are subtle: parsing differences, IPv6, encodings and redirects
Not following redirects breaks some legitimate links, such as URL shorteners
Blocking by network rules needs an egress design that many teams do not have
whenToUse: Any feature where a user, a customer or another system supplies a URL, hostname or address that your server will contact
Webhook delivery, link previews, URL import, document and image converters, and anything that renders a remote page on the server
Treat a redirect target and a DNS answer as input too
whenNotToUse: Do not rely on a deny-list or a regular expression on the URL string as the only control
Do not return the full fetched response to the requester when the feature only needs a yes or no, or a thumbnail
pitfalls: A string deny-list: it stops the spelling you wrote down and nothing else
Checking the hostname but not the address it resolves to, so a name pointing at a private address gets through
Resolving twice, once for the check and once for the fetch, so a changing DNS answer slips between them (DNS rebinding)
Following redirects without re-checking, including those from a trusted host that has an open redirect
An allow-list matched with a substring or suffix test, so a lookalike host passes
Trusting the internal network: services that need no credentials from callers on the inside turn a small SSRF into a large one
Leaving the cloud metadata endpoint open to any local process, so one request can fetch the machine's credentials
Fixing the import feature and forgetting the other places that fetch URLs, such as webhooks and PDF generators

roles.label: Fetcher service
roles.description: Fetches the URL from inside the network.

roles.label: Internal service
roles.description: Metadata endpoint or admin tool that only the inside can reach.

roles.label: DNS
roles.description: Turns names into addresses, and the answer can change.

quiz.question: An image importer refuses URLs whose host is localhost or 127.0.0.1. An attacker submits a public hostname that they control, and its DNS record points at a private address. What happened?
options: The deny-list compared strings, and the dangerous part was the address the name resolved to
The importer should have blocked every URL that contains a dot
HTTPS would have prevented the request from reaching the private address
The deny-list was correct, and the DNS server is the part that was broken
quiz.explanation: A list of bad strings does not see what a name resolves to, so any hostname pointing at a private address is a way around it. HTTPS does not decide where the connection goes, and blocking dots would break nearly every URL.

quiz.question: A fetcher resolves the host, confirms the address is public, then hands the hostname to an HTTP client, which looks it up again and connects to a private address. Which change closes this gap?
options: Resolve the name three times and require that the answers match
Connect to the address that was checked, instead of resolving the name a second time
Lower the timeout of the HTTP client so the second lookup fails more often
Lowercase the hostname before the first lookup
quiz.explanation: The flaw is the gap between the check and the use. Pinning the verified address removes it. Extra lookups can all be answered differently by a record built for this, and a timeout or lowercase does not change which address is used.

quiz.question: A team adds an allow-list containing only their image CDN and feels the importer is safe. The CDN host has an endpoint that redirects to any URL given in a parameter, and the fetcher follows redirects. What is the remaining problem?
options: The allow-list should contain more hosts so that fewer requests are refused
Allow-lists work only for IP addresses and cannot be used with hostnames
The redirect sends the fetcher to a target that was never checked, so redirects need to be off or re-checked at every hop
The CDN should be moved to a different domain name
quiz.explanation: The allow-list was applied to the first URL only. A redirect from an allowed host leads to an unchecked address. Adding hosts or renaming the CDN changes nothing about that, and allow-lists work well with hostnames.
